claims.text: Creating a gradient nanostructured surface layer in a conventional metal can concurrently improve strength and ductility.
Severe plastic deformation, such as surface mechanical attrition treatment, can form a gradient nanograined surface layer.
The resulting structure has a continuous grain-size gradient from a nanostructured surface to a coarse-grained interior.
A nanograined surface increases yield strength.
The nanograined surface increases yield strength by hindering dislocation motion.
A grain-size gradient promotes heterogeneous strain distribution.
The grain-size gradient promotes strain hardening.
The gradient enhances ductility by smoothly transferring deformation from the stiff surface to the ductile core.
Relative to a uniformly coarse-grained metal, a gradient nanostructured metal will have increased yield strength.
Relative to a uniformly coarse-grained metal, a gradient nanostructured metal will have improved uniform elongation.
Relative to a uniformly nanostructured metal without a gradient, a gradient nanostructured metal will have increased yield strength.
Relative to a uniformly nanostructured metal without a gradient, a gradient nanostructured metal will have improved uniform elongation.
Concurrent strength–ductility improvement requires the gradient layer to be sufficiently thick relative to the sample size.
The beneficial effects may diminish when the gradient is too shallow.
The beneficial effects may diminish if processing introduces defects.
The magnitudes of the strength and ductility improvements depend on processing parameters and material-specific responses.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome require improved ductility or increased uniform elongation, but the falsification rule treats unchanged uniform elongation ('no decrease') as sufficient to avoid falsification. Thus, the experimental decision rule does not strictly test the stated improvement claim.
